description: The web player of a music streaming service: playlists, a play queue, search, liked songs and a now-playing bar.

issues.title: Track lengths show as 3:5 instead of 3:05
issues.symptoms: Songs whose length has fewer than ten leftover seconds show a broken time such as 3:5 in playlists, the queue and the now-playing bar.
acceptanceCriteria: A track of 3 minutes 5 seconds is shown as 3:05.
A track of exactly 3 minutes is shown as 3:00.
Durations whose seconds already have two digits, and playlist totals, are unchanged.
hints: Pick a track whose length ends in a single-digit number of seconds and compare what you see with what you expect. Which function turns seconds into text?
The seconds part is converted to text as it is, so 5 becomes "5" rather than "05".
Make sure the seconds part is always two characters wide when it is put after the colon.
In formatDuration, pad the seconds to two digits (for example with padStart(2, "0")) before building the string.

context.affected: Every listener sees it on every track that has single-digit seconds, roughly one song in six. Support gets a steady trickle of "your times look wrong" messages.
context.priority: Medium: very visible and embarrassing, but nothing is broken functionally.
context.outOfScope: Do not change how playlist totals are written (for example "13 min") and do not touch track data.
reproduce: Open the app and the Morning Drive playlist.
Find "Neon Skyline", which is 185 seconds long.
Read the length shown next to the title: it says 3:5.

guide.alex: Every place that shows a track length goes through one helper in src/lib/format.js. trackRow, queuePanel and nowPlayingBar all call it, so start there rather than in the components. Read how it builds the final string from minutes and seconds.
guide.sarah: Try lengths of 0, 5, 59, 60, 61, 65, 180 and 185 seconds. A whole number of minutes is an edge case that is easy to forget. Also check that two-digit seconds such as 754 (12:34) still look right.
guide.daniel: When you glue numbers into a clock-like string, a number has no idea it should be two characters wide. Formatting time usually needs explicit padding so that every value keeps the same shape.

issues.title: Screen readers announce the play/pause button as just "button"
issues.symptoms: Listeners using a screen reader hear only "button" for the main play/pause control in the now-playing bar, while the other controls are announced properly.
acceptanceCriteria: While paused, the play/pause button has the accessible label "Play".
While playing, the play/pause button has the accessible label "Pause".
The rest of the bar (track info and the other labelled controls) still renders as before.
hints: Compare the markup of the play/pause button with the other buttons in the bar. What do the others have that this one does not?
The button only contains an icon character, so it has no text that a screen reader can read.
Give the button an accessible name that matches what pressing it would do right now.
Add an aria-label to the toggle-play button: "Pause" when isPlaying is true, otherwise "Play".

context.affected: Blind and low-vision listeners cannot tell what the main control does. An accessibility audit flagged it as a blocker.
context.priority: High: accessibility audit finding that must be closed before the next release.
context.outOfScope: Do not redesign the bar or change icons, and do not rename the other labels.
reproduce: Turn on a screen reader or inspect the accessibility tree.
Play any track so the now-playing bar appears.
Focus the large play/pause button: its name is empty, unlike Previous track and Next track.

guide.alex: The bar is built by nowPlayingBar in src/components/nowPlayingBar.js, which returns one template string. Look at how the shuffle, previous and next buttons are written and compare them with the toggle-play button. Its icon depends on isPlaying.
guide.sarah: Check both states, paused and playing. The label should follow the state, not be a fixed word. Also make sure the data-action attribute on the button is still there afterwards.
guide.daniel: Buttons that only contain an icon have no readable name for assistive technology. An aria-label supplies the name. Good labels describe the action the control performs, and they change when the control changes.

issues.title: Searching for "daybreak" finds nothing unless you type the capital D
issues.symptoms: Listeners searching their playlist get no results when they type in lowercase, even though the song or artist is right there. Typing the exact capitalisation works.
acceptanceCriteria: Searching by title matches regardless of upper or lower case.
Searching by artist matches regardless of upper or lower case.
Empty, whitespace-only, padded and non-matching searches behave as before.
hints: Search for a track using all lowercase letters, then using its exact capitalisation. Which function decides whether a track matches?
The comparison between the typed text and the title or artist is exact, so "neon" does not equal "Neon".
Both sides of the comparison need to be put in the same case before checking for a match.
In filterTracks, lowercase the trimmed query once and lowercase the title and the artist before calling includes.

context.affected: Almost all listeners type search text in lowercase, so search looks broken for most people. Support has had several complaints this week.
context.priority: High: search is a core flow and the fix is wanted in this sprint.
context.outOfScope: Do not add fuzzy matching, new searchable fields or debouncing.
reproduce: Type "neon skyline" into the search box.
See "No tracks match your search." even though "Neon Skyline" is in the list.

guide.alex: The search box dispatches library/search, which stores the text in state.query. selectVisibleTracks in src/state/selectors.js gets the open playlist tracks and hands them to filterTracks together with the query. The matching rule lives in filterTracks.
guide.sarah: Try the same search in lowercase, uppercase and mixed case, against both a title and an artist. Also try an empty box, only spaces, leading spaces around a real word, and text that matches nothing. Titles with symbols like "&" are worth one try.
guide.daniel: Text comparison is exact by default, and "A" is a different character from "a". Searches are meant for people, so both sides are normally brought to a common form (for example the same case) before comparing.

issues.title: "Play next" adds the song to the end of the queue
issues.symptoms: Choosing "Play next" on a track puts it after everything already in the queue, so it plays last instead of right after the current song.
acceptanceCriteria: "Play next" places the track at the front of the queue.
After the current track ends, the "play next" track is the one that plays.
Adding to an empty queue and "Add to queue" (which appends) behave as before.
hints: Queue three tracks, then use "Play next" on a fourth. Where does it appear in the "Up next" list?
Both queue actions currently do the same thing. They should differ in where the track goes.
"Play next" should put the track before everything that is already waiting in the queue.
In the queue/playNext case of the reducer, build the new queue with the track first and the existing queue after it.

context.affected: Anyone who builds a queue and wants to jump a song ahead, which is common at parties. They say the feature "does nothing".
context.priority: Medium: a visible feature gap, but there is a manual workaround.
context.outOfScope: Do not change "Add to queue", queue removal or shuffle.
reproduce: Play any track and add two other tracks with the queue action.
Look at "Up next": the track is last, not first.

guide.alex: The row buttons are wired up in src/main.js and dispatch actions into the reducer in src/state/reducer.js. The queue itself is just an array of track ids in state.queue. Read the queue/add and queue/playNext cases side by side, then see how player/next takes from the queue.
guide.sarah: Try "play next" on an empty queue, on a queue of one and of several tracks, and twice in a row (the later one should come first). Then press next and check which track plays. Make sure "Add to queue" still appends.
guide.daniel: A list gives you two natural places to put a new item, the front and the back, and the difference is the whole feature. When two operations look almost identical, ask what they are meant to do differently.

issues.title: Likes survive signing out, and liking a track changes data it should not touch
issues.symptoms: After liking some songs and resetting the session for another listener, the same hearts are still filled in. Developers also see earlier snapshots of the state change after a like.
acceptanceCriteria: Liking a track leaves the previous state and the original catalogue data untouched; only the new state shows the like.
Resetting the session returns a state with no liked tracks.
Liking and unliking still updates only the chosen track, the liked list stays correct and unknown track ids change nothing.
hints: Like a track, then reset the session. Also compare the state before and after a like: is anything in the old state different? Which reducer case handles likes?
The like case edits the track object in place and only copies the outer array. Old states and the original seed share that same object.
Reducers must return new objects instead of editing existing ones. The liked track needs to be replaced by a changed copy.

In the track/toggleLike case, build tracks with map: return { ...track, liked: !track.liked } for the matching id and the same object for every other track. Keep returning the same state for an unknown id.

context.affected: Every listener who likes songs and shares a device sees the previous person likes. Engineering also cannot rely on state snapshots, which blocks the undo feature.
context.priority: High: privacy-flavoured bug that also blocks the undo feature planned for next sprint.
context.outOfScope: Do not change how likes are displayed, and do not add persistence or new actions.
reproduce: Open a playlist and like two tracks.
The hearts are still filled in and "Liked songs" is not empty.

guide.alex: Likes are stored as a liked flag on each track object inside state.tracks, and playlists and the queue only hold ids. Start at the track/toggleLike case in src/state/reducer.js, then look at createInitialState and session/reset to see where the track objects come from and who else holds them. selectLikedTracks in selectors.js reads the flag.
guide.sarah: Capture getState() before a like and check it again afterwards. Compare the original seed objects after liking. Try like then reset, like then unlike, two different tracks, a track id that does not exist, and checking that subscribers are still notified when a like happens.
guide.daniel: This is mutation of shared state. If two places hold the same object and one edits it in place, the other changes too, even when you thought you made a new state. Immutable updates copy only what changed and leave everything else alone.
